title: Henry Skaggs, Green River long hunter
summary: Maryland-born Henry Skaggs (1724–1810) was among the earliest long hunters through Cumberland Gap and hunted the Green River country by 1769.
bodyMarkdown:
[Henry Skaggs](/people/#henry-skaggs) was one of the first Long Hunters to work the country west of the mountains. He was born in Maryland on January 8, 1724, to a Scots-Irish father, James Skaggs. The Skaggs men were known as hunters and fur traders.

His career as an explorer began in 1761, when he joined [Elisha Walden](/people/#elisha-walden) on a hunt into what is now northeast Tennessee. Two years later he went deeper into the Cumberland country. In 1764, [according to his biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Skaggs), he led his own party through Cumberland Gap.

Those trips caught the eye of [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone) and of [Richard Henderson](/people/#richard-henderson), the North Carolina land speculator. Skaggs went to work as a land agent and scout for Henderson's company.

In the fall of 1769 Skaggs came back with [Kasper Mansker](/people/#kasper-mansker), [Joseph Drake](/people/#joseph-drake), and [Col. James Knox](/people/#james-knox). They reached the Dix River country and pushed on into the Green River lands. One day they heard a strange sound in the woods near the Barrens. Mansker crept in and found Daniel Boone lying on a deerskin, singing. Boone and his brother [Squire](/people/#squire-boone) hunted with them for a week or two.

Skaggs left his name on the land. Part of the [Wilderness Road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wilderness_Road) across Rockcastle County, from Hazel Patch to Crab Orchard, was known as Skaggs Trace. Skaggs Creek, which runs through Barren County, marks his old hunting range.

In June 1775 he and [Valentine Harman](/people/#valentine-harman) guided [Col. Thomas Slaughter](/people/#thomas-slaughter) through the Green River country for Henderson's [Transylvania Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony).

In 1799 Skaggs led the hunt for the Harpe brothers, frontier killers loose in western Kentucky. One posse after another lost its nerve and scattered, and Skaggs kept going alone. He reached the cabin of [Daniel Trabue](/people/#daniel-trabue) just as Trabue's young son was found murdered by the Harpes. The two men searched for days but never caught them. Trabue's own story is told in [Daniel Trabue of Columbia](/stories/daniel-trabue-of-columbia/).

In 1801 Skaggs claimed 200 acres in newly formed Barren County, probably near present Hiseville. He died there on December 4, 1810. His fellow hunter [James Knox](/stories/james-knox/) worked the same country.

## Kentucky today

Wilderness Road routes through Rockcastle County follow the old Skaggs Trace corridor. In Barren County, Skaggs Creek and the Hiseville area recall his last years, and [Glasgow](/stories/glasgow-the-barrens/) tells the story of the Barrens he hunted.
